<Rep. Joseph D. Morelle>: The Smithsonian American Women's History Museum is long overdue and deserves a place on the National Mall. The National Mall is where our nation tells its story--both its triumphs and its struggles--and American women are main characters in every chapter of that story. That is why Committee Democrats support H.R. 1329, as introduced by Republican Congresswoman Nicole Malliotakis, as well as its companion bill related to the National Museum of the American Latino, H.R. 1330. Notably, H.R. 1329 has 230 cosponsors, including 105 Republicans. H.R. 1330 is similarly bipartisan, featuring 126 cosponsors, 36 of whom are Republicans. Together, these bills correct a statutory anomaly that has stalled both museums and allow them to move forward on the Mall, consistent with congressional intent and prior Committee action.
Unfortunately, Committee Republicans chose to abandon this bipartisan approach and instead politicize legislation that has, for years, enjoyed broad bipartisan support. The amended version of the bill authored by Representative Mary Miller and introduced by the Majority changes the legislation in four key ways:
1. It grants President Donald Trump unprecedented,
unilateral, and unchecked authority to override the
Smithsonian's site recommendation and select a location
of his choosing.
2. It turns control over the museum's design and
construction to boards like the National Capital
Planning Commission, which have been filled by
President Trump with political loyalists.
3. It omits entirely the National Museum of the
American Latino, despite the longstanding bipartisan
understanding that both museums would move forward in
tandem.
4. It inserts a politically charged, ideological
poison pill intended to dictate what the museum can and
cannot say about women's history, undermining
curatorial independence.
During the markup, Committee Democrats offered an amendment to restore the bill to its original, bipartisan form--retaining the Women's History Museum language as introduced and incorporating the Latino Museum fix. The amendment was rejected on party lines, though no justification for doing so was offered by the Committee's majority.
This departure from the bipartisan legislative framework is especially unfortunate in light of the bill's history. In 2019, when this Committee first authorized the Women's History Museum, Democrats accepted an amendment from Representative Loudermilk requiring the museum to reflect ``the diversity of the political viewpoints held by women of the United States.'' That same language appears in this bill and analogous language is in the Latino Museum legislation. The Majority's actions at the markup call into question the consistent application of that principle, to say the least.
If the Majority's objective was to advance this legislation, it would have preserved the broadly supported, bipartisan bills addressing both museums rather than replacing it with a measure that excludes the Latino Museum, constrains curatorial independence, and vests unprecedented decision-making authority in President Trump.
These concerns are exacerbated by recent executive actions seeking to dictate how the Smithsonian presents American history. The issuance of these presidential directives is unacceptable and raises serious questions about political interference in an institution long respected for its curatorial independence.
Committee Democrats remain committed to establishing both the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum and the National Museum of the American Latino on the National Mall-- and doing so in a manner consistent with longstanding bipartisan intent, without poison pills, and without giving the President the right to unilaterally dictate where the museum is located.
Joseph D. Morelle,
Ranking Member.
